newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Christian group alleges big slave trade in Sudan.
newsitem.headline: Christian group alleges big slave trade in Sudan.

text.p: A Swiss-based global Christian organisation alleged on Friday that slave trade existed on a massive scale in Sudan, sponsored in part by the African nation's Islamic government.
Christian Solidarity International (CSI) made its charge in a letter to the United Nations Commissioner for Human Rights, Jose Ayala Lasso.
"All the available evidence points to a massive slave trade in Sudan," said the letter, signed by CSI's international president Hans Stuckelberger, a Protestant pastor.

"There are believed to be tens of thousands of black African children who have been abducted from their families in raids sponsored by the government of Sudan and who are currently enslaved in northern Sudan."

CSI, which often sends representatives to Sudan without the approval of Khartoum, said that in the latest incidents on October 27 the government's Popular Defence Force killed five people and enslaved 20 young women and children.
These attacks occurred in six villages inhabited by black Africans in the Bahr El Ghazal area in the centre of the country on the borderlands between north and south Sudan, it added.

In his letter to Ayala Lasso, Stuckelberger appealed for the U.N. rights chief's help to obtain the freedom of a 10-year-old girl, Abuk Lual, he said had been captured during another raid by the official defence forces in March last year.

Although her brother had been bought out of slavery by CSI official John Eibner during a clandestine visit last month, her owner had refused to accept the normal price for her because he believed she was valuable for "sexual exploitation."

The letter, a copy of which was made available to news agencies in Geneva, said many of the 58 slaves Eibner had managed to buy out told him they were forced to assume a Moslem identity and were often beaten.
In August, U.N. special rights investigator Gaspar Biro was allowed to visit Sudan after a two-year ban imposed because Khartoum objected to earlier reports he compiled on slavery and forced labour.

During his stay, a Sudanese newspaper quoted him as saying there was no signs of slavery being practised in the country. But on his return, he issued an unusual statement saying the Sudanese media had "grossly misrepresented" his views on the situation there.
